title: 2015 HMMT November Guts Problem 29
statement: Find the largest real number \(k\) such that there exists a sequence of positive reals \(\left\{a_{i}\right\}\) for which \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_{n}\) converges but \(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sqrt{a_{n}}}{n^{k}}\) does not.

solutions.text:
Answer: \(\square\)
For \(k>\frac{1}{2}\), I claim that the second sequence must converge. The proof is as follows: by the CauchySchwarz inequality,

\[\left(\sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{\sqrt{a_{n}}}{n^{k}}\right)^{2} \leq\left(\sum_{n \geq 1} a_{n}\right)\left(\sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{1}{n^{2 k}}\right)\]

Since for \(k>\frac{1}{2}, \sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{1}{n^{2 k}}\) converges, the right hand side converges. Therefore, the left hand side must also converge.

For \(k \leq \frac{1}{2}\), the following construction surprisingly works: \(a_{n}=\frac{1}{n \log ^{2} n}\). It can be easily verified that \(\sum_{n \geq 1} a_{n}\) converges, while

\[\sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{\sqrt{a_{n}}}{n^{\frac{1}{2}}}=\sum_{n \geq 1} \frac{1}{n \log n}\]

does not converge.
